def-csm-frontier-mean-field-ensemble.definition_interface:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with the metric $d_1(q,r):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|q(a)-r(a)|$ and its induced topology, called the $\ell^1$ topology. This is a metric: symmetry, nonnegativity and separation follow coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by summing $|q(a)-s(a)|\leq|q(a)-r(a)|+|r(a)-s(a)|$. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the probability measure on Borel subsets $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$ that assigns mass
$$p_{n,\beta}\bigl(\{x^n\in\Omega_n:L_n(x^n)\in B\}\bigr).$$

For a real-valued function $f$ on a nonempty set $S$, define $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\inf_{y\in S}f(y)\}$ and $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\}$; either set is empty if the corresponding extremum is not attained. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $A\subseteq\Omega_n$ and an event $E\subseteq\Omega_n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(E)>0$, define the conditional probability by $p^{\otimes n}(A\mid E):=p^{\otimes n}(A\cap E)/p^{\otimes n}(E)$. For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\geq1$, put $U_m:=\{x\in K:|F(x)|<m\}$. These sets are open by continuity of $F$: if $x\in U_m$, continuity gives a neighborhood on which $|F(y)-F(x)|<m-|F(x)|$, hence $|F(y)|<m$. They cover $K$ because every real $|F(x)|$ is less than some positive integer. By the finite-open-cover meaning of compactness in [A2], finitely many $U_{m_1},\ldots,U_{m_k}$ cover $K$, with $k\geq1$ since $K$ is nonempty. Let $M:=\max\{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$; then $-M<F(x)<M$ for every $x\in K$. Thus $F$ is bounded above and below. This uses the explicitly defined cover and a maximum of finitely many integers, without any simultaneous choice of pointwise neighborhoods. Since $I$ is not identically $+\infty$, choose $x_0\in K$ with $I(x_0)<+\infty$. Therefore $F(x_0)-I(x_0)\leq c\leq\sup_K F<+\infty$, so $c$ is finite. The integrand $e^{nF}$ is bounded above and bounded below by the positive constant $e^{n\inf_KF}$, and $\mu_n$ is a probability measure, hence $0<Z_n<+\infty$ and $\nu_n^F$ is a probability measure.

Let $G\subseteq K$ be open, let $x\in G$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Continuity of $F$ gives an open neighborhood $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq G$ and $F(y)>F(x)-\varepsilon$ for every $y\in U$. Hence $\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq e^{n(F(x)-\varepsilon)}\mu_n(U)$. By [A1], the logarithm of this integral divided by $n$ has liminf at least $F(x)-\varepsilon-\inf_U I\geq F(x)-\varepsilon-I(x)$. Taking the supremum over finite-rate $x\in G$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the open-set integral lower bound $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq\sup_{x\in G}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $C\subseteq K$ be closed and put $c_C:=\sup_{x\in C}(F(x)-I(x))$, with $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. If $C=\varnothing$, its integral is zero and the required bound is immediate. Since $F$ is bounded and $I\geq0$, either $c_C$ is finite or $c_C=-\infty$. Suppose first that $c_C$ is finite, and fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $x\in C$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, lower semicontinuity of $I$ and continuity of $F$ give an open neighborhood $V_x$ on which $F\leq F(x)+\varepsilon$ and $I\geq I(x)-\varepsilon$. Choose a ball $U_x$ centered at $x$ with $\overline U_x\subseteq V_x$. For each $x\in C$ with $I(x)=+\infty$, choose $M>\sup_KF-c_C+1$; lower semicontinuity gives an open neighborhood $V_x$ on which $I>M$, and choose such a ball $U_x$. Take the family of all centered balls satisfying these conditions; it covers $C$. A closed subset $C$ of compact $K$ is compact: adjoining $K\setminus C$ to any relative open cover of $C$ gives an open cover of $K$. Thus finitely many admissible balls suffice, and only finitely many centers and neighborhood witnesses are selected. Put $C_j:=C\cap\overline U_{x_j}$ for the resulting centers. Each $C_j$ is closed. At a finite-rate center,
$$\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq F(x_j)-I(x_j)+2\varepsilon\leq c_C+2\varepsilon;$$
at an infinite-rate center,
$$\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq\sup_KF-M<c_C-1.$$
The integral over $C$ is bounded by the finite sum $\sum_j e^{n\sup_{C_j}F}\mu_n(C_j)$. Applying [A1] to each closed $C_j$ and using that a finite sum has logarithmic limsup no greater than its largest summand gives
$$\limsup_n\frac1n\ln\int_Ce^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq c_C+2\varepsilon.$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the localized bound in this case. If $c_C=-\infty$, every point of $C$ has infinite $I$. For any real $M$, lower semicontinuity gives, at each $x\in C$, an open neighborhood $V_x$ with $I>M$; take all centered balls with closures in such neighborhoods and then a finite subcover of $C$. The corresponding closed pieces $C_j$ then satisfy $\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq\sup_KF-M$. The same finite-sum and LDP argument gives a logarithmic limsup at most $\sup_KF-M$. Since $M$ is arbitrary, this limsup is $-\infty=c_C$. Thus in all cases
$$\limsup_n\frac1n\ln\int_Ce^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq\sup_{x\in C}(F(x)-I(x)).$$

Taking $G=K$ in step 1.2 and $C=K$ in step 1.3 gives $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\geq c$ and $\limsup_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\leq c$, proving the log-Laplace limit. The function $I_F=I-F+c$ is lower semicontinuous, is nonnegative by the definition of $c$, and has compact sublevel sets because those sets are closed in compact $K$. To prove attainment, set $f:=F-I$, which is upper semicontinuous and bounded above by $\sup_KF$. For every integer $k\geq1$, the set $A_k:=\{x\in K:f(x)\geq c-1/k\}$ is closed and nonempty by the definition of $c$; these sets are nested. Compactness gives $\bigcap_{k\geq1}A_k\ne\varnothing$: otherwise their open complements would cover $K$, and a finite subcover would contradict that a nested finite intersection is nonempty. Every point of this intersection has $f(x)\geq c-1/k$ for all $k$, hence $f(x)\geq c$ and therefore $f(x)=c$. Equality $I_F(x)=0$ holds exactly when $F(x)-I(x)=c$, so its nonempty zero set is precisely the stated maximizing set.

For open $G\subseteq K$, apply the open-set integral lower bound from step 1.2 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_G(F-I)-c=-\inf_G I_F$, this is the LDP lower bound for $\nu_n^F$.

For closed $C\subseteq K$, apply the closed-set integral upper bound from step 1.3 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_C(F-I)-c=-\inf_C I_F$, this is the LDP upper bound for $\nu_n^F$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite, let $p$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$, and set $S:=\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{a\in\mathcal A:p(a)>0\}$. Then $S$ is finite nonempty and $p(a)>0$ on $S$. For each $n\ge1$, use the finite product law $p^{\otimes n}$ from [[def-it-finite-alphabet-product-law]] and [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]] on $\mathcal A^n$, and let $X_1^{(n)},\ldots,X_n^{(n)}$ be its coordinate maps. Let $\widehat P_n$ be the empirical type of this coordinate word, viewed as a $\Delta(\mathcal A)$-valued map. Identify the support simplex
$$\Delta(S):=\{q\in[0,1]^S:\sum_{a\in S}q(a)=1\}$$
with the face of $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ whose coordinates outside $S$ vanish. Then $\widehat P_n\in\Delta(S)$ almost surely under $p^{\otimes n}$. For any set $\Gamma\subseteq\Delta(S)$, let $\Gamma^\circ$ and $\overline\Gamma$ denote its interior and closure in the relative topology induced by $\|\cdot\|_1$.
With $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\ge-\inf_{q\in\Gamma^\circ}D(q\|p),$$
and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le-\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p).$$
For every $n\ge1$ the finite upper bound
$$p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le(n+1)^{|S|-1}\exp\!\left(-n\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p)\right)$$
also holds. If the two infima agree, the limit exists and equals their negative common value. Equivalently, when $S\ne\mathcal A$, one may restrict the product sample space to $S^n$ without changing these event probabilities, since every word outside $S^n$ has zero product mass.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous, meaning that $\{x\in K:I(x)>a\}$ is open for every real $a$, and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Here a good rate function is a lower semicontinuous map $J:K\to[0,+\infty]$ whose sublevel sets $\{x:J(x)\leq a\}$ are compact for every real $a$. Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x)):=\{x\in K:F(x)-I(x)=c\}$, with $F(x)-(+\infty):=-\infty$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and let $p$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$. Then $q\mapsto D(q\|p)$ is finite and continuous on the probability simplex $\Delta(\mathcal A)$.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with the metric $d_1(q,r):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|q(a)-r(a)|$ and its induced topology, called the $\ell^1$ topology. This is a metric: symmetry, nonnegativity and separation follow coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by summing $|q(a)-s(a)|\leq|q(a)-r(a)|+|r(a)-s(a)|$. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the probability measure on Borel subsets $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$ that assigns mass
$$p_{n,\beta}\bigl(\{x^n\in\Omega_n:L_n(x^n)\in B\}\bigr).$$

For a real-valued function $f$ on a nonempty set $S$, define $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\inf_{y\in S}f(y)\}$ and $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\}$; either set is empty if the corresponding extremum is not attained. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $A\subseteq\Omega_n$ and an event $E\subseteq\Omega_n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(E)>0$, define the conditional probability by $p^{\otimes n}(A\mid E):=p^{\otimes n}(A\cap E)/p^{\otimes n}(E)$. For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

Write $q(+1)=(1+m)/2$ and $q(-1)=(1-m)/2$. Substituting into [F1] with $p(+1)=p(-1)=1/2$ gives
$$D(q\|p)=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m),$$
with the zero-mass endpoint term omitted. Since $q$ depends continuously on $m\in[-1,1]$ and [F8] makes $D(q\|p)$ continuous on the whole simplex, adding $\beta h(q)=-\beta Jm^2/2$ shows that $\Phi_\beta$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$; [F8] supplies the boundary limit $t\ln t\to0$ behind the convention $0\ln0=0$. The formula is even in $m$.

For $|m|<1$ define $a(m):=\operatorname{atanh}(m):=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+m}{1-m}$. By [F3]–[F5] and direct differentiation, $$a'(m)=\frac1{1-m^2},\qquad \Phi_\beta'(m)=a(m)-\beta Jm.$$ For $0<m<1$ put $g(m):=a(m)/m$ and define $r:[0,1)\to\mathbb R$ by $r(m):=m/(1-m^2)-a(m)$. Then $g'(m)=r(m)/m^2$, $r(0)=0$, and $r'(m)=2m^2/(1-m^2)^2>0$ for $0<m<1$. The mean value theorem [F6] applies to $r$ on $[0,m]$ because $r$ is continuous there and differentiable on $(0,m)$; it gives $r(m)>0$, hence $g'(m)>0$.

The same theorem [F6] applied to $a$ on $[0,m]$ gives $g(m)=a'(c_m)$ for some $c_m\in(0,m)$; as $m\downarrow0$, $c_m\downarrow0$ and $a'(c_m)\to1$, so $\lim_{m\downarrow0}g(m)=1$. As $m\uparrow1$, $(1+m)/(1-m)\to+\infty$, and the increasing onto logarithm [F3] gives $a(m)\to+\infty$, hence $g(m)\to+\infty$. Thus $g$ is continuous, strictly increasing from limiting value $1$ to $+\infty$ on $(0,1)$.

If $\beta J\leq1$, then for $0<m<1$, $\Phi_\beta'(m)=m(g(m)-\beta J)>0$ by step 2.1. The mean value theorem [F6] on each subinterval of $[0,1]$ makes $\Phi_\beta$ strictly increasing there; continuity includes the endpoint $m=1$. Evenness then shows $\Phi_\beta(m)>\Phi_\beta(0)$ for every $m\neq0$, so $0$ is the unique global minimizer.

If $\beta J>1$, the limits in step 2.1 give $a,b$ with $0<a<b<1$, $g(a)<\beta J<g(b)$. Continuity of $g$ on $[a,b]$ and the intermediate value theorem [F7] give an $m_\beta\in(a,b)$ with $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$; strict increase of $g$ makes it unique on $(0,1)$. The derivative formula in step 1.2 is negative for $0<m<m_\beta$ and positive for $m_\beta<m<1$. By [F6], $\Phi_\beta$ strictly decreases on $[0,m_\beta]$ and strictly increases on $[m_\beta,1]$, including the endpoint by continuity. Evenness proves that the only global minimizers on $[-1,1]$ are $\pm m_\beta$; in particular the stationary point $m=0$ is not a minimizer.

The equation $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$ is $\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)=\beta Jm_\beta$. If $r=(1+m_\beta)/(1-m_\beta)$, then $\exp(2\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta))=\exp(\ln r)=r$ by [F3], so the stated formula for $\tanh$ gives $\tanh(\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta))=(r-1)/(r+1)=m_\beta$. Hence $m_\beta=\tanh(\beta Jm_\beta)$. Conversely, any $m\in(0,1)$ solving this fixed-point equation yields $\exp(2\beta Jm)=(1+m)/(1-m)$ by rearrangement of the stated $\tanh$ formula; applying $\ln$ and [F3] gives $g(m)=\beta J$. Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with the metric $d_1(q,r):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|q(a)-r(a)|$ and its induced topology, called the $\ell^1$ topology. This is a metric: symmetry, nonnegativity and separation follow coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by summing $|q(a)-s(a)|\leq|q(a)-r(a)|+|r(a)-s(a)|$. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the probability measure on Borel subsets $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$ that assigns mass
$$p_{n,\beta}\bigl(\{x^n\in\Omega_n:L_n(x^n)\in B\}\bigr).$$

For a real-valued function $f$ on a nonempty set $S$, define $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\inf_{y\in S}f(y)\}$ and $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\}$; either set is empty if the corresponding extremum is not attained. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $A\subseteq\Omega_n$ and an event $E\subseteq\Omega_n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(E)>0$, define the conditional probability by $p^{\otimes n}(A\mid E):=p^{\otimes n}(A\cap E)/p^{\otimes n}(E)$. For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

On $0<u\leq1/9$, $R(u):=(1-u^4)/u^4=u^{-4}-1$ decreases and $1/(1-u^4)$ increases, so $B(u)$ decreases. At $u=1/9$, $R(u)=6560$ and $B(1/9)=12\ln6560-16\cdot6561/6560$. Also $16\cdot6561/6560<17$ by integer multiplication, so $B(1/9)>7$ and $B(u)>0$ throughout $(0,1/9]$. In particular $s''(u)>0$ on that interval. By applying [F6] first to $s'$ and then to $s$, positive second derivative makes $s'$ strictly increasing and every interior chord lie strictly above the graph; hence $s$ is strictly convex on $(0,1/9)$.

Fix $u\in(0,1/10]$ and choose $t>0$ so that $0<u-t<u+t<1/9$, possible because $1/10<1/9$. Strict convexity from step 3.1 gives $s(u-t)+s(u+t)>2s(u)$.
